diagnosis.bottleneck: The query scans the entire payment_type column (≈495K rows) via a sequential scan and then performs a perfect hash aggregation. With only ~5 distinct payment_type values, the aggregation itself is cheap, so the dominant cost is reading and decompressing the payment_type column for every row.

plan_nodes.note: Table: trips | Type: Sequential Scan | Projections: payment_type | Estimated Cardinality: 495833

hypotheses.claim: No known pattern matched; the plan's most expensive operator is the candidate.
The SEQ_SCAN reads all 495,833 payment_type values from disk; if the table is partitioned or sorted by payment_type, partition pruning or a zone-map skip could avoid reading entire row groups.

The PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY processes every row despite extremely low cardinality (5 groups); a pre-aggregated metadata cache or materialized view could answer this query without scanning the fact table.
The compression/decompression projections (nodes 6/7) add CPU overhead per row; using a dictionary-encoded column with direct aggregation on dictionary codes could eliminate the decompress step.
Bypassing the decompression at plan node 6 by aggregating directly on dictionary-encoded payment_type codes will reduce total CPU cycles consumed by the query.
